categories.name: credential_access
categories.description: AD privilege escalation via two mandatory, non-alternative paths — Kerberoasting (Path B) and GPO abuse (Path C) — rather than the simpler valid-accounts reuse of Phases 3a/3b.
hints: The shared-local-admin trick from Phases 3a/3b doesn't work here — these hosts are domain-joined and the foothold account has no local admin rights. You need actual AD privilege escalation, and there are two separate routes, both required.

Path B: enumerate service accounts with SPNs (`Get-ADUser -Filter {ServicePrincipalName -like '*'}` / Rubeus), request a TGS for one, and crack it offline — its ticket is deliberately weakly encrypted (RC4). The cracked account has read rights somewhere useful. Path C, independently: look at GPOs linked to the domain, especially ones that provision a specific non-Windows host — SYSVOL GPP items can carry a recoverable `cpassword`.

Path B: the Kerberoastable account is a member of a group with read rights on the corporate file server (VM3) — crack it with hashcat/john against its RC4 ticket. Path C: the GPO named for provisioning the OT recon host (VM4) has a Scheduled-Task GPP item with a `cpassword` — decrypt it with Microsoft's published GPP AES key (MS14-025) to get that host's login directly. Neither path alone is sufficient; VM3's documents and VM4's credentials are both needed later.

categories.name: recon_ot_enumeration
categories.description: Enumerating the OT device population once inside Subnet 3, after both AD paths and the DMZ pivot.
hints: Once you're on the engineering workstation (VM2) and inside Subnet 3, scan it for hosts speaking IEC 61850 MMS (TCP port 102) — there is more than one.
Three hosts answer MMS on 10.1.3.0/24: 10.1.3.1, 10.1.3.50 and 10.1.3.51. Query GetServerDirectory/GetLogicalDeviceDirectory on each.
Structural inspection alone isn't enough here — cross-check what you find against the semantic answer from the tag database (VM4, reached with Path C's credentials) before picking a target.

categories.name: decoy_avoidance
categories.description: Two-layered device identification: semantic (VM4) and structural (MMS/XCBR), neither sufficient alone.
hints: The tag database on VM4 gives you a plaintext label for which device the plant calls the breaker-control relay — but confirm it structurally too before acting. VM3's share also has a SIPROTEC engineering export (`IEC station 1.scd`) from the last commissioning round, listing each relay's IED name, IP and bay designation — cross-reference that against VM4's asset tags to tie an IED name to a feeder.

Cross-reference the semantic answer (VM4's tag plus the .scd's IED-to-bay mapping) against the actual device's IEC 61850 model: does it genuinely expose an XCBR node, or is the model missing it / showing a different product than the documentation implies?

Only act once the semantic label and the structural check (genuine XCBR under proper IEC 61850 semantics) agree on the same device. An incorrect target is a discoverable, logged trap, not a scenario-ending event.

categories.name: dmz_pivot
categories.description: Reaching Subnet 2 through the Jump Host (VM6), whose credentials now come from VM3 (Path B) rather than a cached VM1c credential.
hints: Subnet 1 has no direct route into Subnet 3 — there's a bastion/session-broker host at the boundary into Subnet 2 that you need credentials for. Those credentials aren't cached anywhere on an IT workstation this time.
The Jump Host (VM6) credentials are embedded in the same correspondence on VM3 that reveals the OT environment — and VM3 itself is only reachable via Path B's cracked service account.
VM6 is reachable at 10.1.1.6 from Subnet 1. Once inside Subnet 2, the tag database (VM4) and the engineering workstation (VM2) are both there — but VM6 itself can't act on OT.

categories.name: semantic_gap
categories.description: Discovering that an OT/SCADA environment exists at all, via VM3's documentation — now reachable only through Path B, not an open share.
hints: Nothing in the domain tells you outright that there's an OT/SCADA environment behind it. The file server (VM3) has the documentation, but it's not just sitting on an open share this time — you need domain-user read rights to get there.
Path B's cracked service account carries read rights on VM3's share specifically — that's the whole point of cracking it. Browse the share once you're in: manuals, network diagrams, correspondence.

VM3's documents reveal that a relay/SCADA environment exists, hint at its network location, and embed the Jump Host (VM6) credentials in the same correspondence — read the emails, not just the PDFs. Among those documents is also a SIPROTEC engineering export (`IEC station 1.scd`), a genuine commissioning artifact naming the IEDs, their IPs and their feeder bays — use it alongside VM4's tag database, not instead of it.
